syllabus.clause: architecture of metadata graphs: pull crawlers vs push/event-based ingestion (change-log streams), search, usage statistics, glossary; open source (DataHub, OpenMetadata, Unity Catalog OSS, Apache Polaris — top-level ASF project since Feb 2026 — as technical catalogs) vs enterprise (Collibra, Atlan, Alation); technical vs business catalog; Amundsen is now low-activity.

Elaborate: a technical catalog answers where a table’s files are and who may read them; a business catalog answers what a column means, who owns it, and where it came from

items.item: at the moment of a search, a push-based catalog already shows a rename that happened hours earlier; a crawl-based catalog still shows the pre-rename state and stays stale until its next scheduled run; a table created and dropped entirely between two crawl runs is never seen by the crawl-based catalog at all, while the push-based catalog records both its create and drop events

Reveal: no -- measured directly, a crawl-based catalog never sees it at all; a push-based one sees both the create and the drop events

items.item: A crawler's staleness window is bounded by its own schedule interval in the worst case (a change happening the instant after a crawl waits a full interval), but this topic's own measurement only demonstrates one concrete point in that range (a Wednesday change against a weekly Sunday schedule), not the general worst-case bound.

at.out: the general worst-case staleness bound named only; this topic's own measurement fixes one specific change time and schedule rather than sweeping the full range

items.item: A push-based pipeline's own event bus (Kafka, in DataHub's real architecture) can itself lag or drop events under backpressure, which would reintroduce a staleness window even in a design that is architecturally push-based -- this topic's toy model applies every event instantly and so cannot demonstrate that failure mode.

at.out: event-bus lag/backpressure as a real push-pipeline failure mode named only; this topic's own toy PushCatalog applies events with zero latency by construction

items.item: A hybrid architecture -- an initial crawl to bootstrap a catalog's state, then push events to keep it current afterward -- is how a real DataHub deployment is usually run in practice, rather than push or crawl operating alone; this topic's measurement treats the two as mutually exclusive to isolate the staleness and visibility difference each one produces on its own.

at.out: the hybrid bootstrap-then-push deployment pattern named only; this topic's own measurement runs crawl and push as separate, non-combined catalogs

items.item: Apache Polaris and Unity Catalog OSS both implement the Iceberg REST Catalog protocol (this chapter's own Chapter 6 §6.3.4 topic covers that protocol directly), which is what lets any REST-catalog-aware engine talk to either one interchangeably -- the technical-catalog category this topic names is defined by that shared protocol, not merely by vendor choice.

at.out: the specific REST Catalog protocol mechanics named only; this topic names Polaris and Unity Catalog OSS as technical catalogs without re-teaching the protocol itself, which Chapter 6 §6.3.4 already covers

items.item: A glossary term in a business catalog is itself a governed asset with its own ownership and review process (who may add or retire a term), not just a label attached to a column -- a detail this topic's own node/edge description of the metadata graph names but does not measure.

at.out: glossary-term governance (ownership, review process for terms themselves) named only; this topic's own measurement covers catalog freshness, not glossary curation workflow

items.item: DataHub's own architecture additionally supports a synchronous HTTP path for metadata changes alongside the asynchronous Kafka path named in this topic's own sources, which matters for a caller that needs an immediate success/failure response rather than fire-and-forget publishing -- a distinction this topic's toy PushCatalog collapses into one instantaneous apply_event call.

at.out: DataHub's own sync-vs-async HTTP/Kafka distinction for push events named only; this topic's toy model applies every push event the same way regardless of transport

items.item: A commercial catalog (Collibra, Atlan, Alation) typically bundles both technical-catalog-style access resolution and business-catalog-style discovery/governance in one product, rather than sitting purely on the business side of this topic's own technical-vs-business split -- the split is a useful lens for the open-source landscape this topic names, not an exhaustive classification of every commercial product.

at.out: commercial-catalog products' own blended technical/business feature sets named only; this topic places them on the business/discovery side of the split as named only, without evaluating their technical-catalog capabilities

items.item: This topic's own catalog entry is itself what topic 13 (the federated governance operating model) later registers an owner and a review cadence against -- the metadata graph this topic builds is not just descriptive, it is the object a later governance process operates on.

A crawler's inability to see a short-lived object is not limited to objects dropped before the next crawl; a crawler can also miss an object renamed and renamed back within one interval, showing no history of either rename at all -- a stronger version of the same blind spot this topic's own temp_export measurement demonstrates with a create-then-drop.

at.out: the rename-and-rename-back variant of the crawl blind spot named only; this topic's own measurement demonstrates the create-then-drop variant specifically

items.item: The syllabus's own "low-activity" wording for Amundsen predates the repository's actual archive notice; this topic explicitly flags that the syllabus is now understating the fact (archived, not merely low-activity) rather than silently teaching the weaker, now-outdated claim as current.
